newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks comments on KLM/Northwest deal.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks comments on KLM/Northwest deal.

text.p: The European Commission sought comments on Wednesday on the proposed alliance between Dutch airline KLM and Northwest Airlines Inc, one in a string of transatlantic air deals it has been probing for months.

In a notice published in the European Union's Official Journal, the Commission said it had not yet reached any position on whether the alliance posed a threat to fair competition. It gave interested parties a month to submit their views.

The Commission's cautious approach in the agreement between KLM Royal Dutch Airlines and Northwest contrasts with the speedy condemnation of the planned link-up between British Airways and AMR's American Airlines.

In July 1996, it started formal investigations into the two agreements as well as the alliances announced by Belgium's Sabena, Austrian Airlines, Swissair and Delta Air Lines, on the one hand, and Lufthansa, SAS, United Airlines, on the other.
It also said it would probe British Airways's ties with USAir, although that inquiry is likely to fall by the way now those airlines have moved apart.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said in a letter to the British government in January that the BA-American alliance would eliminate competition on many key routes between Britain and the United States and has warned London repeatedly since against ignoring the Commission's view.
In January it considered fining KLM and its American partner for failing to provide data on their alliance agreement.

The contracts, ranging from code-sharing, worldwide pricing consultation and a joint venture on flights between Europe and the United States, were detailed in the noticed published in Tuesday's Official Journal.

The Commission said it had not at this stage decided whether article 85 of the treaty of Rome, which bans agreements and concerted practices which distort competition, was applicable to the deal between KLM and Northwest.
The Commission's legal powers to vet transatlantic air deals have been challenged by the British government, but not so much by the other EU national capitals concerned.
